title: Becoming a teacher
hook: the Buddha sends his monks out to wander, and a stranger learns from the way one of them walks

segments.voice: Yesterday: your teachers, Sigala bowing to the directions, and the teacher who checks you understood. Your line: proud of you in public.

A monk named Assaji is walking through the city of Rajagaha on his alms round, bowl in hand. He isn't preaching. He isn't saying anything at all. A young wanderer named Sariputta, a pupil of another teacher who is still searching for the deathless, sees him and stops. Something in the way this monk moves, going forward, looking back, eyes down, calm, makes Sariputta follow him down the street. When the round is done, he asks: who is your teacher, and what does he teach? Assaji says he's new, and can only say a little. A little turns out to be enough.

That scene comes from the Vinaya, the book of the monastic discipline. A little earlier in the same book, the Buddha has a small group of monks who have understood the teaching, sixty, the text says, and he sends them out. Go and wander, he tells them, for the good of the many, for the happiness of the many, out of compassion for the world. And don't let two of you take the same road. So teaching begins as walking: roads, villages, alms rounds, not lecture halls. And the Assaji story shows what that can look like: a person whose way of moving made someone else curious. The lesson started before a word was spoken. The Dhammapada puts the order plainly. In Max Muller's translation: "Let each man direct himself first to what is proper, then let him teach others; thus a wise man will not suffer." Yourself first, then others; the verse doesn't let the second step come before the first. This week looked at teachers near and far, famous and forgotten. Today the arrow turns toward the listener. In this picture, nobody needs a title to teach. Someone who practices is often being watched by someone else: a child, a roommate, a coworker who notices how they handle a bad morning. Becoming a teacher, here, is less a decision than something that happens when practice shows.
screen: `GO AND WANDER, FOR THE GOOD OF THE MANY.`

segments.voice: Let the body settle, upright and easy, the way Assaji might have walked: not stiff, not showing off. Bring to mind one person who will see you today, and pick one small thing you'd want them to catch from you without being told: patience in a line, putting the phone down when they talk, a real thank-you. Don't plan a speech; just let that one thing be the lesson.
Carika. The wandering the Buddha sent his monks on, so that the way they moved taught before they spoke.
Your line: by example. Yourself first, then others, as the verse says. Day one thousand twenty-nine, done.

howItsDone: In Buddhist communities, monastics are expected to teach through conduct as well as words, and many lay Buddhists speak of practice at home and work as the way they pass the teaching on.

fork.setup: you're Assaji. a stranger stops you after your alms round and asks who your teacher is and what he teaches. you're new. what do you do?

fork.reveal: Assaji admits he's new and gives a short answer. it's enough for Sariputta, who goes on to become a great disciple.

original.note: Pali carika: a wandering, a journey on foot; the word the Buddha uses when he sends the monks out.

trapdoor: what you thought: a teacher is someone who decides to teach.
what it means: in these texts, teaching begins with walking and with your own conduct, so the way you move can teach before you speak.
what a scholar hears: caratha bhikkhave cārikaṃ bahujanahitāya bahujanasukhāya, the sending out of the monks in Mahāvagga I.11, and Assaji's bearing in Mahāvagga I.23.

chat.says: I'm not a teacher. How could anything I do teach someone about Buddhism?
options: Assaji said almost nothing; Sariputta followed him because of how he moved.
You can't; only someone with a teacher's title can teach anyone about it.
Teach others first, then work on yourself; that's the order the verse gives.
chat.meaning: Sariputta followed Assaji because of how he walked, before a word was spoken. The Dhammapada says: yourself first, then teach others.

Carika.meaning: wandering: the monks' journeys for the good of the many

notes: Editor: review updated to match the revised day 1028 (Sigala, not SN 45.2); the week recap by title cut, since day 1030 lays out the whole block the next day; 'anyone who practices is already being watched' softened to 'often'; 'tends to sound hollow' (narrator's verdict) replaced with a line about the verse's order.
Dhammapada 158 quoted from Max Müller (SBE 10, 1881); confirm exact wording and punctuation.
'Sixty, the text says': Mahavagga I.10–11 says there were sixty-one arahants in the world (the Buddha included); the script says sixty monks, matching the outline. Confirm.
Mahavagga I.11 paraphrased: 'go and wander for the good of the many ... let not two go the same way.' Rhys Davids & Oldenberg (SBE 13) wording not quoted because the writer was not certain of it.

Mahavagga I.23: Assaji's bearing ('going forward, looking back, eyes down') paraphrased; confirm. 'Goes on to become a great disciple' in the fork reveal is a general description of Sariputta; confirm.

The hook field is rewritten from the index hook ('the Buddha sent out the sixty; every practitioner teaches by example') to avoid the 'every' claim; the voice keeps the outline's idea as 'anyone who practices is already being watched by someone'.
Day 1029 is a week end; the teach looks back at days 1023–1029 by title.
'Teaching that skips the first step tends to sound hollow' and 'mostly isn't a decision' are the writer's framing; soften if needed.
